unit: DAP wire framing and payload-shape mapping: frame, read_message, parse_frame, parse_variable

cases.notes: Content-Length counts bytes of the payload, not characters; for pure ASCII the two coincide.

The payload is 9 characters but 10 bytes: 'ñ' is a 2-byte UTF-8 sequence. A header that counted characters instead of bytes would desynchronize the stream the first time a non-ASCII value appears. This is the byte length the original test asserts, verbatim.

Header is read one byte at a time until the literal 4-byte sequence \r\n\r\n is seen at the tail of the accumulated header buffer; the Content-Length value (38) is then used to read exactly that many body bytes and parse them as JSON.

Two frames placed back-to-back with nothing but their own headers separating them. A reader that buffers past the first message's declared body length would swallow the start of the second message's header. Three sequential calls: first two decode the two objects in order, the third (stream exhausted) returns None — the read_message contract for a closed/ended stream.

id is produced by Value::to_string() on the JSON 'id' field, not a dedicated string extractor — for the number DAP always sends this renders as plain digits ('7'), but would come out wrapped in escaped quotes for a non-conformant adapter that sent a JSON string id instead. line is used exactly as received: the client declared linesStartAt1=true at initialize, so no adjustment happens here. scope_id is always null out of parse_frame itself — it is filled in afterwards by collect_stack once the frame's scopes have been requested.
A non-zero variablesReference is DAP's 'this value is expandable' signal; it is stringified into the app's opaque object_id.
0 is DAP's dedicated 'nothing to expand' sentinel, mapped to object_id: None rather than the string "0".
